note: The characters who come out of the wave in a city (docs/v2/characters.js), one at a time. The cast: each drawn after one of DIRT's artists, from a species in DIRT's grammar of places, with the place's own plants and, among them, its artist's home's (plants.json, artists.json); it lives in its native place (native: its artist's home town, where the species lives; the slug and the hummingbird are no place's) and comes out of a wave only there; pressed, it can be followed through the cities on its artist's map (characters.js, land.js). Drawings in scripts/characters/<id>.py; scripts/build_characters.py writes <id>.json. The daily characters pass (REFINE.md) adds one from the backlog and refines the three refined longest ago.

cast.name: Red fox
cast.why: The most widespread wild carnivore on Earth, and a city animal in London, New York, Paris and Melbourne, so it belongs wherever the site's cities are.

native.why: Cy Twombly was born in Lexington, Virginia (Wikidata P19, characters/homes.json); red foxes live throughout Virginia.
native.source: Lexington is DIRT's Temperate Broadleaf & Mixed Forests, Nearctic, whose grammar gives black bears and coyotes as its hunters, not the red fox (a Palearctic hunter of biome 4 there); the red fox's range covers most of North America, though whether the eastern foxes are native or descend from colonial introductions was long argued (Kamler, J. F. & Ballard, W. B. (2002). A review of native and nonnative red foxes in North America. Wildlife Society Bulletin 30(2): 370-379).

after.why: The artist drew its look himself (14 Oct 2026: "Here is an improved graphic for the fox that represents Cy Twombly"): a pixel fox, three-quarter, on a dark ground with Twombly's chalk loops, crayon dashes in red and cream, and lavender squares. The graphic is the fox: its inks are measured off it (the coat's four oranges, the cream lit and in shade, the plum-brown of its legs and ears, the amber of its eye, the warm grey it shades its cream with), and the other poses the page reads were made as edits of it so all stay in register (scripts/characters/trace_fox.py). DIRT's ground is drawn after Twombly first (dirt/README.md), and no artist on the roster is nearer a fox among plants: his Natural History portfolios (Mushrooms, 1974; Some Trees of Italy, 1976) are botanical plates. Its outline is a chalk line, as he wrote on his blackboards, so it reads on the city's dark ground; the line it leaves is his writing, in the graphic's own chalk, a pale lilac-grey and a cream, a looping pen leaning right, two lines in two inks, lifting between phrases; pressed, it is boxed in red, as he boxed his plates, in the red of Untitled (Roses) and of the graphic's crayon.
works: Natural History Part II: Some Trees of Italy (Title Print)

cast.poses: trot (four frames, diagonal pairs), stand, back (stops and looks back over its shoulder), look (turned to you: the artist's own graphic), sit — each drawn fine, one CSS pixel a cell, 112 by 90 cells
cast.notes: Traced from the artist's graphic and its edits (scripts/characters/trace_fox.py, fox_fine.json), 112 by 90 cells, one CSS pixel a cell: the graphic is its look, the other poses were made as edits of it with OpenAI's gpt-image-2.5 (kept outside the repository, as the chimera's are) and traced down, the inks measured off the graphic, the eyes set by hand. The whole fox has only the five poses the page asks for (its pounce, toss and gekkering are the chimera's parts, still drawn by fox.py's rig, in the new inks). Guessed still: which diagonal of the trot is which (the model draws the gait but its near and far legs are only a shade apart); the trot's four frames are four drawings, so the fur's patches move a little from frame to frame.
log: 2026-10-01 first drawing: three rounds of render and compare (ears restored, legs shortened to a fox's and the body lowered, a fuller brush, a bigger head and longer muzzle, the coat dithered less, the look back lifted clear of the back)

2026-10-01 in the page and the preview: the outline in chalk grey so the black stockings read on the dark city ground, the coat's darkest step kept for the edges between parts (it read as a leopard's spots), no dots small enough to leave gaps; his writing drawn as one continuous looping line behind it

2026-10-14 second pass, three rounds against the real fox and Twombly's hand: the brush no longer a bar of the body's own thickness (narrow where it leaves the rump, fullest past its middle, tapering to the white point), the belly tucked up behind the ribs (the chest its deepest part), and the eye, which had vanished (its amber is the coat's light step), set in a black rim lined on toward the muzzle. Chimera: the fox's three parts checked as head, body and hindquarters beside the deer, squirrel, bison and eagle: the folds still agree

2026-10-14 redrawn from the artist's own graphic (a pixel fox on a dark ground with Twombly's chalk loops, red and cream crayon and lavender squares): the page's fox is now its trace, 112 by 90 cells at one CSS pixel (it was 40 by 26 at two), in the graphic's inks; the trot, the stand, the look back and the sit are edits of it traced the same way; the writing it leaves is the graphic's chalk (pale lilac-grey and cream, not Roman Notes' greens); its trot at 6 frames a second, so a stride of about 20 pixels matches the 58 a second it covers

ethogram.name: mousing pounce
ethogram.what: It stands still with its head cocked, listening for a vole under snow or soil, then leaps in a high arc and comes down nose first. Pounces made facing north-east are far more often successful, which suggests foxes use the Earth's magnetic field to judge the distance.
ethogram.source: Červený, J., Begall, S., Koubek, P., Nováková, P. & Burda, H. (2011). Directional preference may enhance hunting accuracy in foraging foxes. Biology Letters 7(3), 355–357.
ethogram.said: the fox listened, then dived nose first into the ground here

ethogram.name: tossing prey
ethogram.what: Foxes, the young especially, toss a caught vole into the air and pounce on it again, over and over.
ethogram.source: Macdonald, D. W. (1987). Running with the Fox. London: Unwin Hyman.
ethogram.said: the fox tossed something into the air

ethogram.name: gekkering
ethogram.what: Two foxes meet side on, backs arched, ears flat, mouths open, and chatter at each other — the gekker, given in fights and in play.
ethogram.source: Newton-Fisher, N., Harris, S., White, P. & Jones, G. (1993). Structure and function of red fox Vulpes vulpes vocalisations. Bioacoustics 5, 1–31.
ethogram.said: the foxes gekkered, side on, mouths open

cast.name: American bison
cast.why: The grazer of the Nearctic prairie, the herd animal of the open ground; and, after Lascaux, the first animal anyone painted.

native.why: Elaine de Kooning was born in Brooklyn (Wikidata P19); New York is the site's city within 25 km.
native.source: A stretch, said so: DIRT's grammar has the American bison on the Nearctic prairie (biome 8, herds), and New York is Nearctic temperate broadleaf forest (herds: white-tailed deer); the bison's range before 1800 reached western New York State and Pennsylvania, not the coast (Hornaday, W. T. (1889). The Extermination of the American Bison, its map of the original range).

after.why: Her Cave paintings (1983-85), made after the bison of Lascaux and Altamira, and the bulls before them (Bullfight, 1959-60): a few broad, leaning strokes. DIRT's roster gives her grammar 4, strokes, so the bison is laid in strokes, not dithered: each band across the coat a step lighter or darker than the light alone gives. The cave's burnt ochre (her saved works' most vivid ink) for the summer coat of the hindquarters, her umbers for the wool of the hump, head and beard, her warm grey for the chalk line; pressed, it is framed in the ochre.

cast.poses: walk (four frames, the four-beat walk, three feet down at a time), stand, graze (its pause: the head down), look (turned to you), lie (its rest: legs folded under)

chimera.head: Bowed
chimera.gaze: low, to the ground and past it

ethogram.name: into the wind
ethogram.what: In winter storms bison stand and move facing into the wind, heads low, the thick wool of the head and hump taking it. The telling that cattle run before a storm and bison walk through it is ranchers' and guides' observation, widely repeated, not a measured result.
ethogram.source: Meagher, M. M. (1973). The Bison of Yellowstone National Park. National Park Service Scientific Monograph Series 1; the storm saying as ranchers' lore.
ethogram.said: the bison walked on into the wind

ethogram.name: wallowing
ethogram.what: It drops and rolls in bare dust or mud, again and again in the same places, wearing shallow bowls of bare ground — wallows — into the prairie.
ethogram.source: McMillan, B. R., Cottam, M. R. & Kaufman, D. W. (2000). Wallowing behavior of American bison (Bos bison) in tallgrass prairie. Journal of Mammalogy 81(2).
ethogram.said: the bison rolled in the dust and left a wallow

ethogram.name: the rut's head-to-head
ethogram.what: In the rut, bulls face each other, heads down, and push forehead to forehead.
ethogram.source: Lott, D. F. (2002). American Bison: A Natural History. Berkeley: University of California Press.
ethogram.said: the bison met head to head

cast.notes: Side on, 40 by 26 cells. Guessed still: the walk's leg phases are the textbook lateral sequence, not traced from film; the horn is a curved dark spike a few cells long (the lit side of its tip is the chalk edge); the lying pose's folded legs are two capsules.
log: 2026-10-01 first drawing, three rounds of render and compare against the real animal and the artist's hand (the artist, 1 Oct 2026: "I want there to be other animals besides the fox as well")

2026-10-14 second pass, three rounds against the real bison and de Kooning's strokes. The five biggest mismatches, most important first: the coat was one slab with a straight seam between the summer ochre and the wool (the ochre now darkens into wool along a ragged diagonal, the strokes leaning, no longer upright); the hindquarters as tall and as bright as the forequarter (lower and slimmer, the coat's own step); the forelegs thick and alike from top to foot (the wool hangs in chaps over a thin dark lower leg and a hoof); the head small and lost in the mane (larger, a mop over the brow, a curved horn pale only at its tip, a shaggy black beard, a pale muzzle, the eye one whole cell); the stride short (a longer reach, a higher lift). The chimera's bison parts take the same legs, coat and hindquarter; three triples re-rendered, the folds still agree.

2026-10-21 third pass, three rounds against the real bison and de Kooning's strokes. The five biggest mismatches, most important first: the head small and shapeless, its horn a stray pale cell floating above it (a longer, heavier head hung low, a pale muzzle with a step down at its edge, the horn growing out of the mop and dark to its tip, a small ear tuft); the topline a tent (a rounded hump over the forelegs and the back dipping behind it before the rump rises); the hindquarters a broad orange plank (a narrower rump, the near hind leg slimmer); the front-on face with no eyes at all (each had been drawn half a cell off, between the cells' centres: each on a whole cell now), and its horns pale blocks (dark); the coat's plaid of two stroke directions (left: it is her mark). Tried the chimera's finer head, the cape rolling into the forelock, on the whole animal: at one cell it drowned the face in dither and it was dropped. The whole animal's refinements are behind `FINE` in bison.py, so a chimera's body keeps the drawing its folds agree with: only its front-on pose changed (the eyes and horns).

cast.name: Red squirrel
cast.why: The backlog paired Matisse with the grey squirrel, a Nearctic animal; the red is the squirrel of his own country, of the crowns of the Nord where he was born (Le Cateau-Cambrésis), and the grammar's Palearctic troop.

native.why: Henri Matisse was born in Le Cateau-Cambrésis (Wikidata P19).
native.source: dirt/earth/out/grammar.json, biome 4 (Temperate Broadleaf & Mixed Forests), Palearctic, crowns.troops: red squirrels.

after.why: He cut his late pictures out of painted paper (Jazz, 1947; Oceania, the Sky, 1946): flat shapes, one colour each, laid edge to edge with the ground between them. DIRT's roster gives him grammar 9, cut shapes. So the squirrel is cut, not drawn: no outline, no shading, each part one flat ink, and where one piece lies over another a gap of the ground between them, as between two pieces of paper. The yellow of his saved works for the tail, the same yellow worked toward their dark for the coat, their cream for the belly, their dark for the ear tufts and the eye; pressed, it is framed in the yellow.

cast.poses: bound (four frames of the half-bound: gathered, pushing off, stretched, landing), stand, up (its pause: sitting up on its haunches), look (turned to you), eat (its rest: the tail curled up its back, paws at its mouth)

ethogram.name: scatter-hoarding
ethogram.what: In autumn it buries seeds and nuts one at a time in many small caches, pushing each in with its nose and patting the earth down; it finds many again by memory and smell, and forgets some, which grow.
ethogram.source: Wauters, L. A., Suhonen, J. & Dhondt, A. A. (1995). Fitness consequences of hoarding behaviour in the Eurasian red squirrel. Proceedings of the Royal Society B 262, 277–281.
ethogram.said: the squirrel buried something here

ethogram.name: tail-flicking and the spiral chase
ethogram.what: It flicks its tail when alarmed or excited, and squirrels chase each other in spirals round a trunk (in the mating chases of late winter).
ethogram.source: Gurnell, J. (1987). The Natural History of Squirrels. London: Christopher Helm.
ethogram.said: the squirrel flicked its tail

cast.notes: Side on, about 30 by 20 cells of the 40 by 26; the tail a scalloped plume in two papers (yellow, with an orange one laid along it). Guessed still: the bound's frames are drawn from stills of a squirrel crossing a lawn, not traced; the front-on head is a rounded square with two tufts and two eyes; the sitting-up squirrel's head is small.
log: 2026-10-01 first drawing, three rounds of render and compare against the real animal and the artist's hand (the artist, 1 Oct 2026: "I want there to be other animals besides the fox as well")

2026-10-14 chimera pass (the day's random triple, the squirrel's head on the bison's body with the slug's hindquarters): its head, grown to meet the folds' marks, was the biggest mass of the three; a size under now (CHIMERA_SLOT_K head 0.9)

2026-10-15 second pass, three rounds against the real red squirrel and Matisse's cut paper. The five biggest mismatches, most important first: the tail a banana (a tube of one width: now a plume, narrow at the root and fullest toward the tip, cut in yellow paper with its edge scalloped like the lobed fronds of Oceania, the Sea, and a narrower orange paper laid along it); the face a bare dot (the whole animal now wears the chimera's face: the tufted ear, the cream chin, the eye; the eye-ring left to the chimera, where it is more than a white dot; the tuft cut shorter; the front-on face's eyes put on cell centres, they had fallen between cells and vanished); the belly a white dash in the middle of the body (one cream paper now lies along the lower edge from the chest to the haunch, cut to the body's own edge, and down the front of the sitting-up squirrel); the chin floating off the head (cut to the skull); the ear a spike. The chimera's squirrel parts take the same tail, tuft and chin; three triples re-rendered, the folds still agree.

cast.name: Bald eagle
cast.why: The raptor of the Nearctic broadleaf and conifer forests and of the rivers of western Pennsylvania, where Warhol was born.

native.why: Andy Warhol was born in Pittsburgh (Wikidata P19).
native.source: dirt/earth/out/grammar.json, biome 4 (Temperate Broadleaf & Mixed Forests), Nearctic, above.eagles: bald eagle.

after.why: Warhol's Endangered Species (1983) has the bald eagle: a drawn line printed over flat fields of colour, out of register. So the eagle is in flat inks, no dither (a screenprint's plates), with a chalk edge so it reads on the dark ground, and its key line laid again one cell off, down and to the right, in his yellow, showing only where it falls off the colour. The plum-brown dark of his saved works for the body, their cream for the head and tail, their yellow for the bill, the eye, the feet and the key line; pressed, it is framed in the yellow.

cast.poses: fly (four frames of the wingbeat: up, level, down, level), stand, back (looks back over its shoulder), look (its white head turned to you), settle (its rest: wings folded, feathers fluffed)

ethogram.name: mantling
ethogram.what: Over food it has caught, it spreads and lowers its wings round it, hiding it from other eagles.
ethogram.source: Buehler, D. A. (2020). Bald Eagle (Haliaeetus leucocephalus), version 1.0. In Birds of the World (A. F. Poole, ed.). Ithaca: Cornell Lab of Ornithology.
ethogram.said: the eagle spread its wings over what it had

ethogram.name: soaring
ethogram.what: It rides rising warm air on still, flat wings, the primaries spread like fingers, for long spells between perches.
ethogram.source: Buehler, D. A. (2020). Bald Eagle, Birds of the World.
ethogram.said: the eagle rose on warm air, its wings still

ethogram.name: the cartwheel
ethogram.what: In courtship a pair lock talons high up and fall turning over and over, letting go before the ground.
ethogram.source: Buehler, D. A. (2020). Bald Eagle, Birds of the World.
ethogram.said: the eagles locked talons and fell, turning

cast.notes: Side on, 40 by 26 cells. It comes out of the wave standing, then flies up and away; it is the one character that leaves by the sky. Guessed still: the wingbeat is four drawn states (up, half up, down, half down), not film; the far wing is a single dark band; the eye is a yellow cell and a dark one, the iris and the pupil.
log: 2026-10-01 first drawing, three rounds of render and compare against the real animal and the artist's hand (the artist, 1 Oct 2026: "I want there to be other animals besides the fox as well")

2026-10-14 second pass, three rounds against the real bald eagle and Warhol's plates. The five biggest mismatches: the level wing a plank (the beat was one long band swung up and down; now four states of a broad wing, its leading edge through the wrist to the tip, the trailing edge back to the body, the flight feathers four fingers at the tip); the wings too narrow; the head a block (a heavier hooked yellow bill, a dark brow, each eye on a whole cell, in the front view too); the perched bird a penguin (tilted forward, a long white tail hanging, the dark wing tips crossing over it, feathered trousers); the plates flat (two now, the coverts a step lighter than the flight feathers).

2026-10-21 third pass, three rounds against the real bald eagle and Warhol's plates. The five biggest mismatches: the wings narrow blades (a chord of 6.6 cells, five fingers fanned at the tip, the outermost longest); the perched eagle's legs one yellow block (two bare legs apart, toes spread forward, black talons, the feathered trousers above); the eye a dark dot under a dark brow, a stare of no colour (a pale yellow iris with the pupil a cell on toward the bill, and in the front view yellow eyes); the perched back a plain two-tone slab (scalloped covert rows over the folded wing, the line Warhol draws over the plates); the yellow key line printed off register over the feet, so they read noisy (left as it is: it is his misregistration). Its chimera head changed only in the eye.

cast.name: Banana slug
cast.why: The slowest of the grammar's floor animals, a single soft mass of one colour that moves of its own accord.
cast.belongs: No place's native: Ariolimax lives on the Pacific coast of North America and Anish Kapoor was born in Mumbai, so the banana slug never comes out of a wave. It walks its walks, is led and followed (Characters.lead), and is a chimera's part.

after.why: Svayambh (2007): a mass of wax that moves through the museum on its own, slowly, leaving its trace on the doorways; Yellow (1999), a field of one colour with no edge. DIRT's roster gives him grammar 6, stacked fields. So the slug is in fields, not light and shade: stacked bands of one yellow from the dark of the foot's fringe to the pale of its back, flat, the steps clean. The deep yellow of his saved works (his pigment), their pale, their violet-grey dark for the fringe, the spots and the eyes; behind it, a trace of that dark along the ground with a glint in it, drying in steps. Pressed, it is framed in the yellow.

cast.poses: crawl (four frames: a wave along the foot, the body stretching and gathering), stand (tentacles out), reach (its pause: the eye stalks up), look (its head lifted toward you), rest (drawn up short, tentacles in)

ethogram.name: trail-following
ethogram.what: It glides on a wave of muscle along its foot over a film of mucus, slowly, and follows the mucus trails other slugs have left.
ethogram.source: Ng, T. P. T. et al. (2013). Snails and their trails: the multiple functions of trail-following in gastropods. Biological Reviews 88, 683–700.
ethogram.said: the slug left a trail here for others to follow

ethogram.name: courtship
ethogram.what: Two banana slugs circle each other, nosing and lunging, for hours before they mate.
ethogram.source: Leonard, J. L., Pearse, J. S. & Harper, A. B. (2002). Comparative reproductive biology of Ariolimax californicus and A. dolichophallus. Invertebrate Reproduction & Development 41, 83–93.
ethogram.said: the slugs circled each other, and lunged

cast.notes: Side on, 31 by 9 cells of the 40 by 26: a dome-backed body, the sole flat on the ground and pale along its margin. It does not leave the screen: it crawls a while and goes back into the soil a row at a time. Guessed still: the crawl's wave is a single hump; a real slug's foot waves are many and fine; the upper tentacles are drawn in one length.
log: 2026-10-01 first drawing, three rounds of render and compare against the real animal and the artist's hand (the artist, 1 Oct 2026: "I want there to be other animals besides the fox as well")

2026-10-14 chimera pass (the same triple): its long foot as hindquarters ran twice the length of a bison's body and read as a ramp; scaled to 0.8 as a chimera's hindquarters (CHIMERA_SLOT_K hind). The canonical bison-eagle-slug is its own fine drawing and is unchanged

2026-10-15 second pass, three rounds against the real banana slug and Kapoor's stacked fields. The five biggest mismatches: the body a flat slab of one thickness (a dome now: thin at the tail, fullest over the mantle, narrower to a blunt head, the sole flat on the ground); the tentacles one-cell hairs (two upper stalks, near and far, each with a dark bulb at its tip, and a short lower one); the foot's fringe a dark patch under the middle (a pale margin along the whole sole, as the real foot's is); the mantle a plain pale cap (a glossy saddle over the front third with the breathing pore at its edge, laid in the same field with no dark edge, as stacked fields have none); the spots a scatter of single cells (four round spots laid along the body, travelling with it). The chimera's slug parts take the same body; three triples re-rendered, the folds still agree.

cast.name: Red deer
cast.why: The deer of the edges of English woods, Woldgate's and the Wolds'.

native.why: David Hockney was born in Bradford (Wikidata P19); Leeds is the site's city within 25 km.
native.source: dirt/earth/out/grammar.json, biome 4 (Temperate Broadleaf & Mixed Forests), Palearctic, understory.herds: red deer.

after.why: He went home to the Yorkshire Wolds to paint them (Woldgate Woods, 2006; the iPad drawings of the East Riding, 2008-11): lanes and the edges of woods drawn in a bent net of strokes. DIRT's roster gives him grammar 3, a net: even structure, the cells bent, never a grid. So the coat is crossed by a bent net of its darker step. The red of his saved works worked into their olive dark for the coat, their pale for the rump and the antlers, their olive for the hooves and the line; pressed, it is framed in the red.
works: The Arrival of Spring in Woldgate, East Yorkshire, 2011

cast.poses: trot (four frames, diagonal pairs), stand, back (stops and looks back), look (turned to you, antlers either side), lie (its rest: legs folded, head up)

ethogram.name: the antler cycle
ethogram.what: A stag casts its antlers in late winter or spring, grows new ones in velvet through the summer, cleans the velvet off in late summer and carries hard antler through the autumn rut and the winter.
ethogram.source: Clutton-Brock, T. H., Guinness, F. E. & Albon, S. D. (1982). Red Deer: Behavior and Ecology of Two Sexes. Chicago: University of Chicago Press.
ethogram.said: the stag's antlers are as they are this month

ethogram.name: freezing
ethogram.what: Watched, it stops dead, head up and ears turned toward what it has seen.
ethogram.source: Clutton-Brock, T. H., Guinness, F. E. & Albon, S. D. (1982). Red Deer: Behavior and Ecology of Two Sexes.
ethogram.said: the stag froze, watched

ethogram.name: roaring and the parallel walk
ethogram.what: In the rut stags roar at each other, and two well matched walk side by side, step for step, sizing each other up before they fight or one gives way.
ethogram.source: Clutton-Brock, T. H. & Albon, S. D. (1979). The roaring of red deer and the evolution of honest advertisement. Behaviour 69, 145–170.
ethogram.said: the stags roared and walked side by side

cast.notes: A stag, side on, 40 by 26 cells. Guessed still: the antlers are a stylised twelve-pointer drawn thin (a beam, brow, bez, trez and a crown, a cell a tine); the rump patch is a cream block with a ragged edge; the antlers are smaller than a stag's, drawn to fit the picture's top over a head carried high.
log: 2026-10-01 first drawing, three rounds of render and compare against the real animal and the artist's hand (the artist, 1 Oct 2026: "I want there to be other animals besides the fox as well")

2026-10-14 second pass, three rounds against the real red deer stag and the artist's hand. The five biggest mismatches: the antlers a grey slab (the chalk outline had filled the air between the one-cell tines: a part can now be drawn with no edge, `noline`; thin branching tines in pale bone, scaled to fit the picture's top); the neck thin and the head small (the whole stag's neck and head larger, the chimera's slots as they were); the body short and square (longer, the belly rising to the flank); the legs thin with no step in them (the lower legs a darker step, a longer reach and a higher lift in the trot); the rump patch a block (small, ragged at its edge).

2026-10-21 third pass, three rounds against the real red deer stag and Hockney's net. The five biggest mismatches: the neck short and the head low (a longer neck, the head carried higher, in the trot and the stand); the antlers, which cannot be tall now that the head is higher (a smaller crown, 0.62 of the old set; tried sweeping the beams further back and it read as a pale bar, so they stay a crown); the ears small and lost against the antlers (big leaf ears held back); the rump patch a small ragged block (larger, running down the thighs); the legs' dither noisy at the hocks (left: it is his net). The whole animal's refinements are behind `FINE` in deer.py: a chimera's parts are byte for byte as they were.

cast.name: Starling murmuration
cast.why: The grammar's one animal that is a field and not a body: thousands of common starlings at dusk, each following its nearest neighbours, so that a turn runs through them as a wave and they move as one mass, a line poured and flung over the sky.

native.why: Jackson Pollock was born in Cody, Wyoming (Wikidata P19, characters/homes.json); Cody is the site's city within 25 km. Common starlings live there now, and are the town's birds as they are everywhere on the continent.
native.source: A stretch, said so: DIRT's grammar has the starling murmuration in the Palearctic broadleaf forest (biome 4, above.flocks), and Cody is Nearctic desert and xeric shrubland, whose grammar gives coyotes. The common starling is no native of North America: about sixty were released in New York's Central Park in 1890 and about forty more in 1891, and it now breeds across the continent (Cabe, P. R. (1993). European Starling (Sturnus vulgaris). In The Birds of North America, No. 48. Philadelphia: The Academy of Natural Sciences; Washington, D.C.: The American Ornithologists' Union).

after.why: His pours of 1947-51 (Number 14: Gray, Brown and Silver II, Number 7) are one line poured and flung over the whole sheet, thickening to a pool, thinning to a thread, drops thrown off it, with no edge and no centre. DIRT's roster gives him grammar 7, scattered marks: dense marks in every direction. So the starlings are not one animal drawn in his hand but the field itself: a murmuration is a poured line that turns as one, a ribbon that thickens into a mass and thins to a thread, each bird one flung mark (a V, a bar, a caret as its wing beats; the far ones a speck), no outline, because a flock has no edge. The umber of his saved works for the birds in shade, their warm grey and off-white for the lit ones, and the ochre (his most vivid ink) flecked through it as thrown paint; pressed, it is framed in the ochre.

cast.poses: trot (eight frames: the flock flying, a ribbon thickening to a head with waves of density running forward through it and the tail curling), stand (eight: wheeling in place, a pinwheel of three arms turning), back (eight: the head of the flock curling up and over, a wave about to break), look (eight: a ring opened toward you with one bird of the ochre at its middle), sit (eight: the pour thickening into a pool, and starlings standing on the ground, heads up and down, a wing flicked); every pose moves

ethogram.name: the murmuration
ethogram.what: At dusk, before they roost, thousands of starlings fly as one mass, each bird following the seven or so nearest to it and not every bird within some distance, so a turn begun at the edge runs through the flock as a wave.
ethogram.source: Ballerini, M. et al. (2008). Interaction ruling animal collective behavior depends on topological rather than metric distance: evidence from a field study. PNAS 105(4), 1232–1237; Attanasi, A. et al. (2014). Information transfer and behavioural inertia in starling flocks. Nature Physics 10, 691–696.
ethogram.said: the starlings turned as one

ethogram.name: probing
ethogram.what: On the ground it walks rather than hops, pushing its closed bill into the turf and opening it there to find leatherjackets and other insects.
ethogram.source: Feare, C. (1984). The Starling. Oxford: Oxford University Press.
ethogram.said: the starling probed the ground, and found something

ethogram.name: the song
ethogram.what: A singing male raises the feathers of his throat, opens his bill and flicks his wings out and in, to a rival or a mate: a long run of whistles, rattles and the borrowed calls of other birds.
ethogram.source: Feare, C. (1984). The Starling. Oxford: Oxford University Press.
ethogram.said: the starlings sang at each other, their wings flicking

cast.notes: A murmuration drawn as a field, 80 by 48 cells at two pixels (160 by 96), every pose of eight frames and living (moves.live): about 260 birds a frame laid on a ribbon, a ring or a disc, each by its place (far a cell, near a V of five), the light from the upper left on the side of the ribbon that faces it. Its drawing is run-length coded (rle). Guessed still: which bird is lit is the ribbon's side, not a measured flock's; the V is the sign for a bird in flight, not a starling's own silhouette (its single bird is the chimera's part, drawn whole).
log: 2026-10-14 first drawing: a murmuration as a poured ribbon after his pours (a line that thickens to a mass and thins to a thread, flung marks, no edge), five poses of eight living frames; the single starling for the chimera

2026-10-15 second pass, three rounds against murmuration footage and Pollock's pours. The flock was a scatter of sparks, not a mass (a third more birds in every pose, the middle layer fuller; the poured skein, a one-cell thread in the dim umber, now runs the whole length of the ribbon in the walk and the wave, not only its thin end); the dark birds were holes on a dark city ground (the coat's steps lifted, the darkest from #3a322d to #4b4239, no far bird in the darkest step, a tenth of the middle birds black or darkest where it was three tenths); the five poses still read apart as silhouettes at 1×: a teardrop, a disc, a crescent, a ring, a stream into a pool.

cast.name: Ocellated lizard
cast.why: A horizon: the Catalan lizard on Dalí's own scrub coast, still on a long flat ground. Europe's largest lizard, in the dry scrub, the stone walls and the old olive groves of the Empordà, where Dalí was born (Figueres) and where the Pyrenees fall to the sea at Cap de Creus.

native.why: Salvador Dalí was born in Figueres, in the Empordà (Wikidata P19, characters/homes.json); the ocellated lizard lives throughout the Iberian peninsula.
native.source: dirt/earth/out/grammar.json, biome 12 (Mediterranean Forests, Woodlands & Scrub), Palearctic, floor.frogs: ocellated lizards; range: Wikipedia, Ocellated lizard (Geographic range: found throughout the Iberian peninsula).

after.why: DIRT's roster gives Dalí grammar 13, the composition after the shore at Cap de Creus in The Persistence of Memory (1931): a landscape in bands, a horizon, its reflection, a fall of flecks. So the lizard is laid in flat bands, not shaded (a back netted in black, a flank of ochre where the blue eyes fall in a row like flecks, a pale belly), and it stands on a long flat ground: a horizon under its feet and, below it, the same bands upside down, broken by the water, fading in a few rows. His dark and near-black for the net, a grey-olive worked from his grey-teal toward the gold of his saved works for the back, the gold itself for the flank, his sand for the belly, the pale of his sky for the ocelli and the reflection.

cast.poses: trot (four frames, diagonal pairs, the tail swinging), stand, back (its pause: up on its forelegs, the head raised), look (its head turned to you), sit (basking, flat to the ground, an eye lidded) — each with its reflection below the ground line; 100 by 40 cells at one CSS pixel a cell

ethogram.name: holding a territory
ethogram.what: In spring the males hold territories and fight for them in the breeding season. A male facing a rival rears up on straight forelegs and gapes before it comes to a bite: the threat display large lizards give, a widely told observation, drawn here, not measured.
ethogram.source: Wikipedia, Ocellated lizard (Reproduction: "Males are territorial in spring and fight in the breeding season").
ethogram.said: the lizard held its ground here

ethogram.name: tasting the air
ethogram.what: It flicks its tongue as it goes, bringing particles of air and ground to the organ in the roof of its mouth that smells them.
ethogram.source: Schwenk, K. (1994). Why snakes have forked tongues. Science 263, 1573–1577.
ethogram.said: the lizard tasted the air

ethogram.name: the bite
ethogram.what: Rival males meet head to head, gape, and bite at each other's heads and necks, hard enough to wound; the fights are the males' business of the breeding season. How large lizards fight is a widely told observation, drawn here, not measured.
ethogram.source: Wikipedia, Ocellated lizard (Reproduction); Description ("a robust lizard … the male has a characteristic broad head … thick, strong legs").
ethogram.said: the lizards gaped, and bit

cast.notes: Side on, 100 by 40 cells at one CSS pixel a cell: the ground line at row 29 and, below it, the reflection (the lowest rows mirrored, the nearest dark, then the pale of the sky, broken by the water and faded by a regular dither over nine rows) in every pose. The bands are flat: the back's net is the edges of a jittered grid (black lines round rosettes of olive), the flank ochre with five blue, black-ringed ocelli each a little lower than the one before, the belly sand. Guessed still: no photograph was reachable, so the proportions are the drawn lizard's (its tail is a little over half its length, where the real one's is two thirds), the legs' joints are a two-bone reach (the near and far legs of a stride are a shade apart), the ocelli's blue is the pale of his sky made bluer (his saved works have no blue), and the front-on head is a rounded wedge with two golden eyes. Its poses beyond the five the page reads (act, play, ritual) are the chimera's and the corpse's.
log: 2026-10-15 first drawing, three rounds of render and compare against the real animal and the artist's hand (the backlog's top: Dalí, the ocellated lizard). Round one: 40 by 26 cells at two pixels was too coarse for a lizard (a net, ocelli, toes), so it is drawn at one pixel a cell, as the red fox is; the shape found (a wedge head with a swollen cheek, a thick neck, a trunk eight pixels deep, legs with the knee forward and the elbow back, long clawed toes, a tail that tapers to a whip), the bands laid (a back netted in black, an ochre flank, a sand belly) and the reflection under the ground line. Round two: the trunk too deep and the legs pillars (a slimmer trunk, longer legs, the body raised); the back too grey (a grey-olive worked from his grey-teal toward his gold); the ocelli too big and black-ringed (smaller, lower in the flank); the cheek a gold mask (an olive crown, an ochre cheek, a pale chin). Round three: the near legs' lit edges ochre so the limbs read against the body; the front-on head larger and higher; the basking lizard's tail laid on the ground. Its chimera parts (the head a fifth larger, the hindquarters with a shorter tail), its corpse rule (a territory: every stop within 400 km of the leg's first), its ritual (the gape and the bite), its published walks, and a door to it from a life's place and a studio ("Follow the ocellated lizard").

cast.name: Anna's hummingbird
cast.why: Stacked fields: the gorget's colour soaks and floods as it turns, the way her stain soaks the canvas. The grammar's one hummingbird for the Nearctic scrub and chaparral of the Pacific coast: a bird that hovers, darts and backs away, and whose throat is rose only where the light is where it is turned.
cast.belongs: No place's native: Anna's hummingbird lives on the Pacific coast of North America (and has spread east into Arizona and north into British Columbia: the article's account of its range, recalled and not re-read on 21 Oct 2026, when Wikimedia answered 429 — to be checked), and Helen Frankenthaler was born in Manhattan, a place the American bison (after Elaine de Kooning, born in Brooklyn) already has: a place has one native character. So the hummingbird comes out of no city's wave. It comes in Frankenthaler's own places (a studio or a place of her life, as the fox comes in Picasso's and the lizard in Dalí's), walks its walks, is led and followed (Characters.lead), and is a chimera's part. Berkeley's and Santa Monica's own hummingbirds are the generated ones, after Mary Corse and Mark Bradford.

after.why: DIRT's roster gives Helen Frankenthaler grammar 8, poured stains: soft marks that flow one way (the soak-stain of Mountains and Sea, 1952, thinned paint soaked into raw canvas so that the colour is in the weave and its edge feathers into the ground). So the hummingbird is stained, not shaded: the rose of its gorget soaks out of the throat into the bronze of its back along a soft dithered edge, a wash of cream thins up the flank, and the wings are the fans they leave in the air, a wash of plum densest at the stroke's edge and thinning back. Her plum-brown for the wings, tail and bill, her gold worked toward the plum for the bronze of the back, her cream for the dusky belly, her terracotta worked toward the gorget's rose for the soak; the gorget is rose only where the light is where it is turned (blazing facing you, dark when perched), which is the stain's own trick.

cast.poses: trot (four frames: darting, the body level, the wings stained across the air), stand (four: hovering, tilted, the wings beating), back (four: backing away, upright, the wings level at the sides), look (four: facing you, the gorget blazing), sit (eight: perched on a twig, wings folded, the gorget dark; the head turns, the tail flicks, the eye shuts) — 64 by 48 cells at 1.5 CSS pixels a cell; every pose plays on the clock

ethogram.name: the display dive
ethogram.what: A male climbs high above a female or a rival and dives steeply, and at the bottom of the dive, as he passes, spreads his tail: its outer feathers flutter and make a sharp chirp (the sound is the tail's, not the voice's). The dive is among the fastest of any bird for its size, some 27 m/s, about 385 body lengths a second.
ethogram.source: Clark, C. J. & Feo, T. J. (2008). The Anna's hummingbird chirps with its tail: a new mechanism of sonation in birds. Proceedings of the Royal Society B 275, 955–962; Clark, C. J. (2009). Courtship dives of Anna's hummingbird offer insights into flight performance limits. Proceedings of the Royal Society B 276, 3047–3052.
ethogram.said: the hummingbird dived here, and its tail sang

ethogram.name: feeding at a flower
ethogram.what: It hovers at a flower and takes nectar with a tongue that is not a tube: its two grooved tips open in the nectar and trap it, many times a second; it takes small insects as well.
ethogram.source: Rico-Guevara, A. & Rubega, M. A. (2011). The hummingbird tongue is a fluid trap, not a capillary tube. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 108, 9356–9360.
ethogram.said: the hummingbird fed here

ethogram.name: the territorial chase
ethogram.what: Males defend a feeding territory: a rival that comes into it is met with a chase, the gorget flared, round and round the flowers until one leaves. How the chase goes is a widely told observation, drawn here, not measured.
ethogram.source: Russell, S. M. (1996). Anna's Hummingbird (Calypte anna). In The Birds of North America, no. 226 (males defend feeding territories); Wikipedia, Anna's hummingbird (Behavior), recalled and not re-read on 21 Oct 2026 — to be checked.
ethogram.said: the hummingbirds chased each other round

cast.notes: Side on, 64 by 48 cells at 1.5 CSS pixels a cell (the bird about 40 cells long), every pose of four or eight frames that play on the clock (moves.live). Guessed still: the wing is not drawn feather by feather but as a plum blade and the stained fan of its stroke (a dithered wash in blocks of two cells, densest at the wing's edge now), the hover's wing positions are chosen for how they read, not filmed; the tilt of a hovering body (38 degrees) and the level body of the chimera's part are the model's; the gorget's colours are the terracotta of her palette worked toward the real rose, and the back's bronze is her gold worked toward her plum, so the bird reads bronze where the real back is green. The real bird's description (length, plumage, the gorget's flares, the white spot behind the eye) is from the English Wikipedia article as remembered: Wikimedia's API answered 429 on 21 Oct 2026 and the article was not re-read, so check it against the article before trusting a detail; the ethogram's papers (Clark & Feo 2008; Clark 2009; Rico-Guevara & Rubega 2011) are cited as recalled, not re-read either.
log: 2026-10-21 first drawing, three rounds of render and compare against the real bird and Frankenthaler's stain (the backlog's top: Helen Frankenthaler, Anna's hummingbird). Round one, the biggest mismatches: the body a rod (a teardrop now, a deep chest narrowing to the vent), the tail a plank as wide as the body (a squarer tail half the body's width, drooped from the rump, its outer feathers tipped pale), the wing a thin stick (a long curved blade, broad at its root, its stroke a stained fan: a wash of plum densest at the wing's edge and thinning back, in blocks of two cells, so it reads as a soak and not a net), the gorget's edge a checker (a feathered dither, the rose soaking back along the throat into the bronze), the eye fused to the bill (a dark eye with a gold glint, a white spot behind it, the bill starting a cell clear). Round two, the other poses: the pause (back) first drew the head turned right round and the bill vanished against the wing, so it is the bird backing away, its body upright and its wings level at the sides (a hummingbird flies backward); the front-on look (the gorget blazing, the wings out either side as two fans, the tail spread under); the perch (a twig, the wings folded to the tail, the gorget dark: it is rose only where the light is where it is turned, eight frames with a head turn, a tail flick and a blink); the display dive (a climb, a hang at the top, head first with the tail spread, out of it with the wings open), the flower (the tongue out and in) and the chase. Round three, the chimera: drawn level on a twig, with tiny feet down to the ground line, the legs thickened so they do not read as pins, the wings folded as hindquarters (a beating wing cut at the hip fold floated), the tail shortened as hindquarters, CHIMERA_SCALE 1.12; checked as head (bison, hummingbird's head, slug), body (bison, hummingbird, fox) and hindquarters (fox, deer, hummingbird). Its row: it is no place's native (Anna's lives on the Pacific coast, Frankenthaler was born in Manhattan, which the bison has), so it comes in her own places, in a walk (Frankenthaler by hummingbird, two published), followed, and in a chimera; its corpse rule is the dive (a climb: the next stop 1,200 km or more away; a fall: the one after within 400 km of the first), its meeting the chase.

2026-10-14 wild boar after Turner, four rounds against the real animal and his strokes: a wedge not a loaf (shoulders raised, hump, narrower haunch, a long tapering snout with its tusk, the head low on a thick neck, the tail hanging) and the coat dark bristly brown, not the pale beige the artist's light palette had washed it to (hands.ladder)

2026-10-14 grey wolf after Monet, three rounds: the tail carried low and straight with a dark tip (it rode up like a fox's), bushy; a ruff and pale cheeks; a broader head, heavier paws; the pale belly now pale (its ladder had come out mid-grey)

2026-10-14 American black bear after Artschwager, three rounds: black, not pale grey (hands.ladder worked the steps toward the artist's lightest by a third each, so every dark animal washed out); rump a little higher than the shoulders, no hump; head carried low and larger, bigger round ears, long flat paws

2026-10-14 coyote after Turrell, three rounds against the real animal and his plates. The five biggest mismatches, most important first: the tail carried up like a fox's brush (low now, bushy, a dark tip); the head carried high in the trot (a coyote trots with it low, near the line of the back: a canid plan's new neck_trot); the muzzle short and thick and the ears small (a long narrow snout, large ears, broad at the base head on, no longer spikes); the build a stocky dog's (lankier: longer, slimmer legs, a narrower chest); the coat's markings straight edged (the saddle's lower edge ragged, the belly's stepped: every species with a saddle or a pale belly gains) and a pale ruff and cheeks. A seated canid's chest and head are a little larger. Wolf, jackal and fennec fox checked beside it.

2026-10-14 mule deer after Serra, three rounds. The five biggest mismatches: the gait was a trot (a mule deer stots: all four feet leave the ground and come down together, the legs stiff, the body low on landing, up, at the top, down: a new quad gait, stot, seven frames a second); the antlers a dark clump that hid behind the ear (they fork, and each fork forks again, in pale bone, drawn over the ear with no edge; every antler kind's radii raised to a cell so its tines stop dropping out); the tail a pale blob (a narrow white rope with a black tip); the face one grey block (a dark forehead over a pale muzzle and cheeks) and the ears small; the neck too long and the head too high, its antlers clipped by the picture's top (a short thick neck, the head carried level, a stockier body). The legs of every cervid are a step slimmer (the moose keep theirs). White-tailed deer, moose and reindeer checked beside it.

2026-10-14 greylag goose after Rembrandt, three rounds. The five biggest mismatches: in flight the wings were blades that left the picture (a broad wing in four states, up, coming down swept back, down, lifting, its flight feathers a darker plate with fingers at the tip: the bird plan's, so every flying bird gains); the body held flat like a duck's (breast high, tail low: every goose, swan and pelican); the bill and legs drawn in the eye's brown (the species' accent is its orange, in Rembrandt's nearest ink); the neck short and the head small (longer, thicker, larger); the bill missing head on (a wedge as broad as the bill is). Canada goose, pelican, golden eagle, turkey vulture, snow bunting and scarlet macaw checked beside it.

2026-10-15 white-tailed eagle after Tuymans, rounds against the real bird and his plates (50 places have it, Bonelli's, the golden eagle and the red-tailed hawk share its plan). The biggest mismatches: the tail a stick (a short broad wedge spread at its end, white in this species: the raptor plan's `tail_fan`); the flight feathers one ink with the wing (a darker plate: `dark_parts` primaries); the wing too narrow for the bird (broader, 22, on a body a sixth smaller: `wing_span`, `scale`). Still weak: the flying frames read as a lump, the wing held in by the picture's height. Vultures and owls have their own plans and were checked beside it, unchanged.

2026-10-15 Iberian lynx after Garaizabal, rounds against the real cat and his modelled bands. The two biggest mismatches: the ear tufts too long (a lynx's are short, a cell and a half, dark at the back of the ear: `ear` 1.5, the mark `earback`) and no cheek ruff (a pale ruff and cheeks: `ruff` 0.9, the mark `cheeks`). The Eurasian and the Canada lynx gain the same; the bobcat does not (its tufts are the older, longer ones). Still weak: a 40 by 26 cat reads by its silhouette, so the spots and the tail's black tip are one or two cells.

2026-10-15 ant after Rauschenberg, five rounds against a real ant and his plates (21 places have an ant: the red wood ant, the red harvester ant, the plain ant). The five biggest mismatches, most important first: the legs (the hind feet were put ahead and the front behind, the body sat low, so six short stubs crossed under it; now the hips under the alitrunk, the feet behind for the hind legs and ahead for the front, the knees found from the two bones and bent outward, the body held high, walking in tripods); legs and feeler drawn with a chalk edge so a cell-wide line became a three-cell cobweb (a new role `limb` in hands.py: one ink, no chalk, which every hand lays); the head a vertical chalk bar fused to the thorax (a round head on a narrow neck, a dark eye with a glint on the lit side, mandibles); the whole ant too small to read (drawn half as large again as its unit, 1.5); the feeler a stub (a scape up and forward, an elbow, a funiculus bent down). Hand-checked in Boulogne's, Genoa's, Manchester's and Carmel's hands. Still weak: the legs are the coat's own mid brown, so on a soil of that brown they quiet down.

backlog.why: Dots: points of light in the dark, as his silver prints hold light.
Stacked fields of sky: a skein crossing an evening light.
The decisive moment: a deer that stops at the edge of the frame and is gone.
